title: Turla
summary: Turla is one of the longest-documented espionage intrusion sets, assessed by multiple governments and vendors as associated with Russian state security services, most commonly linked in public reporting to the Federal Security Service. That association rests on third-party analysis of infrastructure, tooling, and targeting, and although several national authorities have stated it with high confidence, it remains an attribution judgement rather than an observable technical fact. Reporting describes targeting of government and diplomatic entities, military organisations, research and defence-industrial bodies, and, in later campaigns, entities in Europe, the Middle East, Asia, and North America. The group is known in public reporting for technically distinctive tradecraft: satellite-based and hijacked-network command and control paths, including abuse of other actors' infrastructure; the Snake framework, a long-lived modular implant documented extensively in national advisories; DNS-based covert channels; custom rootkit components; and the use of compromised legitimate websites and cloud services to blend with normal traffic. It has also been reported to co-opt and operate implants on networks already compromised by other intrusion sets, which means victim telemetry may show two distinct actors and incident scope must be established carefully. For defenders, the group's emphasis on low-and-slow collection and network-layer concealment makes host-only monitoring insufficient. Detection effort should include DNS anomaly analysis, hunting for long-lived encrypted sessions to unexpected destinations, review of egress paths for unauthorised tunnels, and integrity monitoring of core system components. Attribution of this cluster should be presented with explicit confidence language, and the overlapping vendor naming schemes should be reconciled before comparing campaigns.
objectives: Describe how hijacked network infrastructure and DNS covert channels complicate network-layer attribution.
Build detections for DNS tunnelling indicators and long-lived anomalous encrypted egress sessions.
Explain the operational risk of acting on a network that a second, unrelated intrusion set has also compromised.
Assess endpoint integrity monitoring options for detecting kernel-level or boot-level persistence.
Evaluate egress filtering and outbound allow-listing as controls against covert channel abuse.
Interpret national advisory attribution language and translate confidence levels accurately into internal reporting.
Prioritise log sources for a low-and-slow espionage threat with multi-year dwell time.
Explain why decommissioning a legacy implant requires both host remediation and infrastructure-side action.
